reason: The supplied proof’s claim that one can always remove elements to enter \([190,210]\) is unjustified and false. The explicit \(24,24,24,24,24,23,23,23,23\) list disproves \(N=10\); the minimal-subset-sum argument proves the corrected answer \(N=11\).
text:
The smallest value is \(\boxed{11}\).

Necessity: For \(N=10\), let the first player write five copies of \(24\) and four copies of \(23\). Their total is \(5\cdot24+4\cdot23=212\). Every proper subset has sum at most \(212-23=189\), while the whole list has sum \(212\). Hence no subset sum lies in \([190,210]\). Thus \(N=10\), and consequently every smaller \(N\), can fail.

Sufficiency: Consider any legal list. Among all its subset sums that are at least \(189\), let \(s\) be the smallest. Such a sum exists because the sum of the whole list is at least \(200\). Adding elements one at a time until the running sum first reaches \(189\) produces a subset sum at most \(188+25=213\), so \(189\le s\le213\).

Suppose \(s>211\). If \(s=213\), then removing any selected element must reduce the sum below \(189\), by the minimality of \(s\). Thus every selected element is at least \(25\), so all are \(25\); but no sum of copies of \(25\) equals \(213\), a contradiction. If \(s=212\), the same argument shows that every selected element is at least \(24\). Eight such elements have sum at most \(8\cdot25=200<212\), whereas nine have sum at least \(9\cdot24=216>212\), again impossible. Therefore \(s\le211\).

Hence every legal list has a subset sum \(s\in[189,211]=[200-11,200+11]\). Therefore \(N=11\) is sufficient and minimal.
